prompt: Which dimension of colour answers "which colour family is it?"

choices.why: Saturation says how much colour there is against grey.

choices.text: Hue, an angle round a circle
choices.why: Right. Red, green, blue: an angle round a circle.
Lightness says how light or dark.

choices.text: The RGB value of the red channel
choices.why: One channel of RGB is how a screen mixes, not which family a colour belongs to.

prompt: Which dimension of colour should carry a quantity on a chart?

choices.why: Right. Everybody sorts light to dark the same way.

choices.text: Hue, because it offers the most distinct colours
choices.why: Distinct is not ordered: the hue circle has no start.
Saturation orders weakly and is better kept for emphasis.
Changing hue as well adds categories the data does not have.

prompt: What is saturation best used for in a chart?

choices.why: That is hue's job.
No colour dimension shows exact values; numbers do.
Right. One vivid colour among muted ones is where the eye goes.

choices.text: Making the series look equally important
choices.why: Equal saturation everywhere wastes the one channel of emphasis.

prompt: On the hue circle, red is at 0 degrees. At about how many degrees is blue?
Pure yellow and pure blue both have HSL lightness of 50%. How do they look?

choices.why: That is what HSL claims, and the eye disagrees.

choices.text: Blue a little lighter than yellow
choices.why: Blue is nearly as dark as black.

choices.text: It depends only on the screen
choices.why: Screens vary a little; the thirteenfold difference survives any of them.
Right. Their luminances are 0.93 and 0.07.

prompt: Which light carries the most weight in relative luminance?

choices.why: Red has 0.2126.
Blue has the least, 0.0722.

choices.text: The three equally, a third each
choices.why: That is closer to how HSL averages, and it is what the eye disagrees with.
Right, 0.7152 of the total.

prompt: A designer picks six category colours at HSL saturation 100% and lightness 50%, round the hue circle, so that none stands out. What happens?

choices.text: All six are equally prominent, as intended
choices.why: Equal in HSL is not equal to the eye.

choices.text: They are all too dark to read
choices.why: Yellow at that setting is nearly as bright as white.

choices.text: Nothing, because hue cannot affect lightness
choices.why: In HSL, changing hue changes real brightness a great deal.
Right. Yellow and cyan glare; blue sinks towards black.

prompt: What does "perceptually uniform" mean for a colour space?

choices.text: Every colour has the same lightness
choices.why: A space contains colours of every lightness.

choices.text: Equal distances look like equal differences
choices.why: Right. That is what CIELAB and OKLab aim for.

choices.text: It uses only the colours a printer can produce
choices.why: That describes a printer's gamut, not uniformity.

choices.text: It describes colours with three numbers
choices.why: RGB and HSL use three numbers too, and are not uniform.

prompt: A seven-step ramp built from equal steps of HSL lightness was measured in OKLab. What did the measurement show?

choices.why: That was the OKLCH ramp, not the HSL one.
Both ramps kept one blue hue.

choices.text: Uneven steps: big at one end, bunched at the other
choices.why: Right. The line of perceived lightness bent.

choices.text: That the ramp was too short to judge
choices.why: Seven steps were enough to see the bend.

prompt: Which of these palettes were designed in perceptual spaces and tested for even steps?

choices.why: Right, along with the ColorBrewer palettes.

choices.text: A rainbow from red to violet
choices.why: A rainbow has uneven lightness, which lesson 12 shows.
HSL is exactly what is not uniform.
Those are usually chosen for logos, not for charts.

prompt: The polar form of OKLab, giving lightness, chroma and hue, is called ___.
colours.py reported a luminance of 0.928 for yellow and 0.072 for blue. How many times brighter is yellow, to the nearest whole number?
Why does colours.py undo the screen's gamma before computing luminance?

choices.text: Brightness adds up only in linear light
choices.why: Right. The weights apply to linear values.
It reads it in one line.
Size is not the reason.
HSL works on the screen's values directly.

prompt: What does turning a chart grey test?

choices.why: Speed is not the point.

choices.text: Whether its palette works by lightness
choices.why: Right. Colours that relied on hue alone turn into the same grey.

choices.text: Whether its axis starts at zero
choices.why: Grey does not change the axis.
Grey tests the colours, not the data.

prompt: A brand's two official colours, a red and a green, have luminances of 0.21 and 0.22. What should a chart that uses them for two series add?

choices.text: Nothing, since red and green are opposite hues
choices.why: Opposite hues with equal lightness are the classic failure, lesson 14.

choices.text: A second cue, such as labels or line styles
choices.why: Right. In grey, or to many readers, the two are almost identical.
The background does not separate two colours of equal brightness.
Saturation does not fix equal lightness.

prompt: The grid has a column of greys, then hues round the circle starting from red, with light rows at the top. Find each of these.

labels.text: a grey with no hue at all

hint: Each column moves 30 degrees round the circle.

prompt: Match each colour description to what it is.

pairs.right: how a screen mixes three lights
easy to pick with, wrong about lightness
the brightness the WCAG formula measures
lightness, chroma and hue as the eye sees them

right_distractors: a palette that is always colour-blind safe

prompt: Put these fully saturated colours in order of luminance, darkest first.
hint: Green carries most of the weight.

prompt: What is HSL still good for?

choices.why: That is where it fails most.

choices.text: Deciding whether text reads on a background
choices.why: That needs luminance.
Right, as long as lightness is checked another way.

choices.text: Measuring how bright a colour looks
choices.why: Its lightness ignores the eye's sensitivity.
